extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of poetics (writers of tragedy and epic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing tragic and epic poetry with attention to plot unity, diction, metaphor, word-formation, and the metrical/linguistic units that shape poetic style. Emphasises what kinds of words and figures suit different genres and how to balance clarity with poetic distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (plot unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ... ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single-action structure makes the poem 'one whole' like a living organism and produces the proper pleasure. Distinguish narrative/epic compositions (which may record events in a period) from a unified dramatic plot. Episodes may be admitted (e.g., Catalogue of Ships) but the central action must remain single and complete. Avoid composing a poem by simply concatenating multiple unconnected actions or contemporaneous events that do not contribute to a single result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and episode-use in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: He never attempts to make the whole war of Troy the subject of his poem ... It would have been too vast a theme ... he detaches a single portion, and admits as episodes many events from the general story of the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For epic (epoieia) keep scope moderate: detach a coherent portion of a larger story and use episodes to diversify without breaking unity. Excessive attempt to cover an entire vast sequence makes the work over-complicated or unwieldy; manage length by limiting the portion treated as a single whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought — effects produced by speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech, the subdivisions being — proof and refutation; the excitation of the feelings, such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought in dramatic speech should produce rhetorical effects (argument, emotional stimulation, impression of importance/probability). Dramatic incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition, while effects intended in speech should be produced by the speaker. The line between incident and spoken Thought matters: do not rely on speech to convey what the action itself can show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Modes of utterance (command, prayer, question, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Utterance. ... it includes, for instance,—what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the modes of utterance is essential for delivery and for shaping characters' lines; however, Aristotle notes this province properly belongs to the art of Delivery. Poets should know and apply these modes so that speech performs the intended function (e.g., commands perform as commands). Misapplication is a fault of delivery rather than poetry per se, but poets must still craft lines with the proper mode in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of linguistic units and metrical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in general includes the following parts:— Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should understand letters (vowels, semi-vowels, mutes), syllable formation, connecting words, and how these interact with metre. Detailed features (aspiration, length, accent, syllable composition) bear on metrical choices. The poet must consider phonetic and metrical properties when forming diction and verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity without meanness (perfection of style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for perspicuity (use of current/proper words) but avoid the 'mean' or commonplace. Clarity comes from using familiar expressions together with judiciously chosen distinctive forms. Avoid pure banality as well as obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced infusion of unusual (strange/rare/metaphorical/ornamental) words
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain infusion, therefore, of these elements is necessary to style; for the strange (or rare) word, the metaphorical, the ornamental, and the other kinds above mentioned, will raise it above the commonplace and mean, while the use of proper words will make it perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix current/proper diction (for clarity) with metaphorical, ornamental, lengthened, contracted, or rare words (for distinction). A style composed wholly of metaphors is a riddle; wholly of strange words is jargon. Use unusual elements sparingly and with purpose to elevate the diction without obscuring meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in employing licenses (lengthening, contraction, alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing contributes more to produce a clearness of diction that is remote from commonness than the lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthening, contracting, and altering words give distinction and can increase clarity by providing recognized deviation from the ordinary idiom. Use these licenses, but not obtrusively — excessive or self-conscious manipulation becomes grotesque or ludicrous (examples: Eucleides' caricature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obtrusive or ludicrous use of rare forms and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such license at all obtrusively is, no doubt, grotesque; ... even metaphors, strange (or rare) words, or any similar forms of speech, would produce the like effect if used without propriety and with the express purpose of being ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use rare words, forced metaphors, or arbitrary word-formation for their own sake; they should serve the poetic purpose. Examples show critics and comic ridiculers seize on obtrusive usage. Judgement and restraint are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as the highest stylistic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius, for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastering metaphor — perceiving apt resemblances and transferring names suitably — is central to poetic excellence. Though teachable techniques exist (types of transfer), the true faculty of producing effective metaphors is a creative ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and methods of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genus→species, species→genus, species→species, and analogical transfers; qualify by adding the related term when needed. Examples: 'the cup of Dionysus'/'the shield of Ares'; 'old age the evening of life.' Metaphors may be refined by proportion/analogy when exact terms do not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of word-types to poetic genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry, indeed, all these varieties are serviceable. But in iambic verse, which reproduces, as far as may be, familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select word-forms to suit genre: dithyrambs favor compound names; heroic poetry tolerates/benefits from rare and lengthened forms; iambic prefers language close to prose (current/proper, metaphorical, ornamental). Adjust diction to the mimetic aim of the metre and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, and altered words
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never been even in local use, but is adopted by the poet himself. ... A word is lengthened when its own vowel is exchanged for a longer one, or when a syllable is inserted. A word is contracted when some part of it is removed. An altered word is one in which part of the ordinary form is left unchanged, and part is re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices can create distinction and should be used as stylistic licenses in measured ways. Provide examples (e.g., newly-coined: ἐρνύγες for 'horns'; lengthening: πόλεως → πόληος; contraction examples). Critics may censure them, but used sparingly they add character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of purely private idiom or excessive dialect-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of ... strange (or rare) words is either a riddle or a jargon ... The strange (or rare) word, the metaphorical, the ornamental ... will raise it above the commonplace and mean, while the use of proper words will make it perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not render diction obscure by mixing too many private expressions, dialectal forms, or foreign usages. Maintain enough shared/common expression so that meaning remains clear; employ dialectal or 'barbarous' usages only where they serve a purpose and do not make the text unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflexion and grammatical form as expressive tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflexion belongs both to the noun and verb, and expresses either the relation 'of,' 'to,' or the like; or that of number ... or the modes or tones in actual delivery, e.g. a question or a command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inflexions (cases, verb forms) deliberately to mark relations of time, number, and speech-mode. Grammatical choices affect meaning and delivery (e.g., interrogative vs imperative forms) and must be considered part of rhetorical and dramatic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence/phrase unity and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sentence or Phrase is a composite significant sound, some at least of whose parts are in themselves significant; ... A sentence or phrase may form a unity in two ways—either as signifying one thing, or as consisting of several parts linked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sentences to serve either as a single unified signification (definition-like) or as a coherent linkage of parts. Sentential unity contributes to clarity and to the rhetorical/poetic effect; not every poetic group needs a verb, but it should form an intelligible unit.
